learning_objective: 🎯 Understand what makes our planet valuable! Learn how to classify resources, why sustainable development is the need of the hour, and explore India's diverse soil types.

main_concepts.simple_explanation: Everything in our environment which can be used to satisfy our needs, provided it is technologically accessible, economically feasible, and culturally acceptable.

Resources are classified by Origin (Biotic vs Abiotic), Exhaustibility (Renewable vs Non-Renewable), Ownership (Individual, Community, National, International), and Status of Development (Potential, Developed, Stock, Reserve).

Development should take place without damaging the environment, and it shouldn't compromise the needs of future generations. 'Agenda 21' was signed at the 1992 Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro to achieve global sustainable development.

Soil is the most important renewable natural resource. Major types in India: Alluvial (most fertile, Khadar & Bangar), Black (Regur, good for cotton), Red & Yellow, Laterite (leached, good for cashew/tea), Arid, and Forest soils.

The washing away of soil by water or wind. We can prevent it using techniques like Contour ploughing (ploughing along slope lines), Terrace farming (cutting steps on hills), and Shelterbelts (planting lines of trees to break the wind).

fun_activity.title: 🔍 The Soil Detective
fun_activity.instructions: Go to a nearby park or garden. Take a pinch of soil and rub it between your fingers. If it feels gritty, it has sand. If it feels smooth and sticky when wet, it has clay. India's famous Alluvial soil is a perfect mixture of sand, silt, and clay!

exam_tips: 📌 Know the difference between Khadar (new, fine, very fertile alluvium) and Bangar (old, coarse alluvium with kankar nodules).
📌 'Black soil' is deeply associated with cotton cultivation and is found in the Deccan trap region (Maharashtra, Gujarat). It has high moisture-retention capacity.
📌 Remember Mahatma Gandhi's quote: 'There is enough for everybody's need and not for any body's greed.' It is frequently asked in the context of resource conservation.
quick_recap: ⭐ National resources include all land within political boundaries and oceanic area up to 12 nautical miles (22.2 km) from the coast.
⭐ Laterite soil develops in areas with high temperature and heavy rainfall, undergoing intense leaching.
⭐ Resource planning in India involves identification, evolving a planning structure, and matching it with national development plans.
